---
title: "Individual-CI filename advisory (rcicr 0.4.0–1.2.3)"
---

This page is an advisory about a bug in rcicr that could save an individual classification
image under another participant's filename. It sets out which versions carried it, how to tell
whether your own stored results are affected, what it does to an analysis, and how to repair
affected output.

**The bug is in versions 0.4.0 through 1.2.3 — 0.4.0 only if you installed it on or after
2017-08-15, see "Which versions were affected" below — all of them GitHub-only, and is fixed in
[1.3.0](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/releases/tag/v1.3.0). It never reached CRAN: the
last CRAN release, 0.3.4.1, predates the option involved by thirteen months, so nothing
installed with `install.packages('rcicr')` was ever affected.**

## This is the bug

The bug is very specific to one function, which is `generateCI()`. When called with
`participants = ...` and `save_individual_cis = TRUE`, it could save each participant's
classification image under a different participant's filename. The images themselves were
computed correctly; only the file names were wrong.

## Which versions were affected

It affects versions 0.4.1 through 1.2.3 outright, all of them GitHub-only.
**Version 0.4.0 is a special case**: it lived only on the `development` branch, from
2016-10-26 to 2021-09-23, and the bug entered partway through that window, on 2017-08-15 — so
whether a 0.4.0 install is affected depends on exactly when you got it, not the version string
alone (see
[`individual-ci-mislabelling.md`](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/blob/main/notes/individual-ci-mislabelling.md)
for the install-date table). Any of these versions is only actually affected whenever
participant IDs weren't already in sorted order (e.g. "p10" sorting before "p2", the ordinary
case from the tenth participant on).

However, `batchGenerateCI()`, `batchGenerateCI2IFC()`, and `generateCI2IFC()`, the route most
tutorials recommend for per-participant CIs, are not affected by the bug. If that's what your
analysis used, this doesn't apply to you. The group classification image that `generateCI()`
returns is also unaffected; only individual filenames from the direct call could be wrong.

## What this does to an analysis

The mislabelling breaks the link between a classification image and the participant it came
from. What that costs depends on what the images were then used for.

If they were averaged into a group image, or looked at without reference to whose they were,
nothing downstream changed: the group CI is a mean over participants and does not depend on
their order.

It matters where a participant-level variable was joined to the images — the common
second-stage design, in which naive raters judge each individual CI and those judgments are
related back to the source participant's condition, score or group. That join was made against
a shuffled set of labels, so whatever the analysis found, it was not computed on the pairing it
was reported as.

On average it costs an effect rather than inventing one. That is a claim about a permutation and
easy to get wrong in either direction, so it is measured rather than argued:
[`tools/simulate-mislabelling-impact.R`](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/blob/main/tools/simulate-mislabelling-impact.R)
runs 20,000 iterations per cell at α = 0.05, and
[`individual-ci-mislabelling.md`](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/blob/main/notes/individual-ci-mislabelling.md#what-it-did-to-a-second-stage-analysis)
writes the results up. Three findings.

**Where there was no association to begin with, the mislabelling does not raise the false
positive rate.** Rejection stays at the nominal 5% in every design tested and at every sample
size, which is structural rather than a lucky set of draws: permuting one side of a pair that is
independent of the other leaves it independent.

That is a statement about the rate, and it is not the same as saying your own result is safe.
The two analyses disagree about significance far more often than the matching rates suggest —
in the null cells they reach a *different* verdict on roughly 9% of datasets, about half of
those being a rejection the correctly labelled data would not have given. The bug does not
manufacture false positives across a literature; it can certainly have handed one to a
particular study, and a result that only became significant on mislabelled files is exactly
that case.

**Where there was a real association and the labelling order has nothing to do with the variable
joined to the images, it is weakened in proportion to how badly the ordering was scrambled.**
That last part is what decides whether your own result is dented or gone, and it follows from
how far your participant vector departed from sorted order. At 50 participants with a real
correlation of 0.5, which a correctly labelled study detects 97% of the time:

| how the identifiers were ordered | share still correctly paired | detected once mislabelled |
|---|---|---|
| one pair out of sequence | 0.96 | 0.949 |
| two pairs out of sequence | 0.92 | 0.924 |
| five pairs | 0.80 | 0.818 |
| ten pairs | 0.60 | 0.560 |
| every pair transposed | 0.00 | 0.081 |
| `p1 … p50` in collection order | 0.02 | 0.047 |

So a couple of participants entered out of sequence costs a few percentage points of power,
while the common `p1 … pN` scheme lands near the bottom of that table: at 12, 20, 30 and 50
participants exactly one file still carries its own participant, detection falls from 97% to 5%,
and the surviving 5% splits evenly between positive and negative, which is what chance looks
like. In that case the other 95% are false negatives — a real association, sitting in the data,
that the analysis can no longer see — which is why the likeliest casualty of this bug is a real
finding that did not appear, in a study filed away rather than published.

Don't read your own case off those sample sizes, though: how much survives is not a smooth
function of N, because it turns on where the identifiers change width. At 99, 100 or 101
participants eleven files keep their own participant rather than one — at N = 100 they are `p1`
and `p80` through `p89` — while at 120 it is back to one. Compute yours instead, from the
participant vector in the order you originally passed it:

```r
ids <- unique(participants)
mean(sort(ids) == ids)   # share of files that kept their own participant
```

That is the left-hand column of the table above, so it places your own analysis on it directly.
`1` means the filenames were correct.

**The exception is a covariate that tracks labelling order** — IDs assigned in collection order
while conditions ran in blocks, or an ID encoding testing date or cohort. There the permutation
is no longer arbitrary with respect to the design, and the residual can come out either sign: a
d = 0.8 condition difference survives attenuated and correctly signed at N = 50 (detected 79% of
the time, 26% once mislabelled), and comes back **reversed** at N = 20, where 14% of runs are
significant in the wrong direction against 0.1% in the right one.

**Where a nuisance trend runs along collection order, the shuffle can also hand back apparent
support**, so this is not a case of noise only. If conditions were assigned in alternating
order, the correct pairing spreads that trend evenly across them and the permutation unbalances
it: hypothesis-consistent significant results rise *above* what the correctly labelled analysis
gives, in 9 of the 12 cells tested and by a factor of four at N = 12. Contiguous condition
blocks behave the opposite way, the trend already being maximally aligned before the shuffle,
which is why both are simulated.

The sign the permutation pushes is fixed by the identifier scheme and the assignment scheme
together, and nothing in lexical sorting refers to a hypothesis. Whether that sign agrees with
what a given study predicted is therefore not something these simulations can answer: each one
fixes the trend and the "predicted" direction as positive rather than sampling them, so nothing
here supports a claim about how often the two coincide across a literature. Naming conventions,
condition coding and the direction of the usual nuisance trends could well be related to each
other in practice, and that would have to be studied rather than assumed.

What is clear is the consequence for one analysis: an affected result can be significant in the
predicted direction and is still not evidence for anything, having been computed on the wrong
pairing. No single affected analysis can be cleared on the strength of an average:

- **A null result from an affected analysis may be an artifact of the shuffle.** If the
  association was really there, this is what removed it. It is also the outcome least likely to
  have been published, so an affected analysis that "didn't work" is worth re-running before it
  is written off.
- **A significant result from an affected analysis is not evidence for the hypothesis it was
  read as supporting**, because the pairing it was computed on was wrong. It needs re-running
  against corrected filenames before it means anything.

Separately, a figure showing individual CIs labelled by participant, condition or group is
wrong as printed, whatever the accompanying statistics did.

Re-running usually costs only the analysis: the images are correct and the filenames are
repaired by renaming (below), so nothing needs regenerating. The exception is a design in which
the wrong filenames determined what happened during data collection, rather than only how the
results were filed afterwards — a participant shown "their own" CI picked out by filename, or
blocks of stimuli assembled by condition from those labels. Renaming cannot reconstruct a
response that was collected against the wrong image, and those observations have to be
collected again.

## How you can quickly check whether this affects you

**Look for an `individual_cis/` directory in your output.** Nothing else in the package writes
one, so finding it means the affected call ran. It is also how to tell which route your
analysis took: the batch functions above pass `participants = NA` and never set
`save_individual_cis`, so they cannot produce that directory, and only a direct `generateCI()`
call can.

Not finding it clears the analysis only if the output still sits as the run left it. A
directory that was renamed, folded into an archive, or had its PNGs moved elsewhere will not
answer to that name any more. The filenames are then a clue rather than a verdict: an
individual CI is `ci_<participant>.png`, but `generateCI(save_as_png = TRUE, filename = ...)`
takes whatever filename it is given, so a group CI saved as `filename = "p3"` is also
`ci_p3.png`. Confirm a loose file against the script that wrote it, or against the data, before
treating it as an individual CI — running the recovery below over a set that is really
something else would scramble output that was correct.
[`individual-ci-mislabelling.md`](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/blob/main/notes/individual-ci-mislabelling.md)
has the table of what in the package writes which filename where.

Do not rely on searching your scripts for `save_individual_cis` instead. It is the sixth
argument of `generateCI()`, so a positional call such as
`generateCI(stim, resp, "face", rdata, pids, TRUE, ...)` sets it without the name appearing
anywhere, and `do.call()` hides it the same way. Grepping and finding nothing does **not**
clear an analysis.

If the directory is there, the ordering of your participant IDs decides it. Run

```r
identical(unique(participants), sort(unique(participants)))
```

using the participant vector in the order you originally passed it. `TRUE` means the files
were named correctly. If it's `FALSE`, the images are still correct; only the filenames are
swapped, and the mapping to fix them is exact (no need to recompute anything, see below).

## How to fix it

If you're affected, the file named `unique(participants)[i]` actually holds the classification
image for `sort(unique(participants))[i]`, so this recovers the correct filenames without
recomputing anything (two steps, so the rename doesn't overwrite a file it hasn't renamed yet):

Work on a copy, and satisfy yourself first that `targetpath` below points at the output of the
run these `participants` came from. The `stop()` calls catch a filename that is missing; they
cannot catch a directory that is simply the wrong one. A different run holding the same
participant identifiers would rename cleanly, permuting a set that had been correct.

```r
# The targetpath you originally passed to generateCI(). If you never passed one, it
# was "./cis" by default in every affected release up to 1.2.1, so the files are in
# "cis/individual_cis/" relative to where you ran the analysis, not in the working
# directory itself.
targetpath <- "./cis"

old <- unique(participants)         # names the files currently carry
new <- sort(unique(participants))   # participants they actually contain

dir <- file.path(targetpath, "individual_cis")
step1 <- file.rename(file.path(dir, paste0("ci_", old, ".png")),
                      file.path(dir, paste0("ci_", old, ".tmp")))
if (!all(step1)) stop("Rename failed for: ", paste(old[!step1], collapse = ", "))

step2 <- file.rename(file.path(dir, paste0("ci_", old, ".tmp")),
                      file.path(dir, paste0("ci_", new, ".png")))
if (!all(step2)) stop("Rename failed for: ", paste(old[!step2], collapse = ", "))
```

(This assumes `sort()` orders your IDs the same way the original run did — always true on the
same machine/session, and true for numeric or lowercase-ASCII IDs like `p1`/`p12` regardless.
It can differ under a different locale if your IDs mix case, accents, or punctuation; check
`Sys.getlocale("LC_COLLATE")` against the original run if you're unsure, or recover on the
machine that produced the files.)

(use the `antici_` prefix instead of `ci_` if you generated anti-CIs).

If you plan to keep using the package, get the fixed version from
[GitHub](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr) (`remotes::install_github("rdotsch/rcicr")`; a CRAN
submission is in progress but not live yet).

More detail:
[`individual-ci-mislabelling.md`](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/blob/main/notes/individual-ci-mislabelling.md)
has the full technical background (every affected version, its dates, and exactly which
configurations trigger the bug), and [issue #267](https://github.com/rdotsch/rcicr/issues/267)
is the pinned advisory tracking this on the repository.

## Personal note

I wrote rcicr in 2014, then left academia in 2017 and stopped maintaining it. I had other
responsibilities and no time for something that felt part of a previous life. Recently I
decided to see if AI would be able to maintain the package, and this week it found this bug.
I'm glad it did, and I consider it the right and scientific thing to do to fix it and announce
it publicly. I don't have the time to do more than that, so if you're still active in this
field and would like to maintain this package, I'd gladly hand over the reins.
